title: Cryptocurrency & Digital Assets Fundamentals
tagline: Understand coins, tokens, stablecoins, wallets and risk, and learn to judge a token before you trust it
summary: A clear, sceptical introduction to cryptocurrency and digital assets: what money is for, the main kinds of digital asset, wallets, exchanges and real trading costs, measuring risk and volatility, reading tokenomics, doing due diligence, and keeping within the rules. Spreadsheet labs let you calculate returns, fees and vesting. This is education, not investment advice.

modules.title: Money and crypto
modules.summary: What money is for, how digital money developed and where cryptocurrency fits.
modules.outcome: You can name the functions of money, describe how digital money evolved and judge claims that crypto is 'the future of money'.
modules.intro: To judge cryptocurrency fairly you first need to be clear about what money does. This module builds that base, then places cryptocurrency on the long road from shells and coins to bank apps.

topics.title: What money does
topics.html:
Barter needs a 'double coincidence of wants': the baker must want what the shoemaker has, exactly when the shoemaker wants bread. Money removes that problem. Anything can become money if people agree to accept it, but good money does three jobs.

The three functions
FunctionMeaningStrong when
Medium of exchangeAccepted in paymentMany people and shops accept it, payments are cheap and fast
Store of valueKeeps purchasing power over timeIts value is stable, not eroded by inflation or wild swings
Unit of accountA common yardstick for prices and debtsPrices are quoted in it and it changes slowly
Useful properties of good money
PropertyWhy it helps
DurableIt does not rot or wear out quickly
PortableEasy to carry or send
DivisibleCan pay large and small amounts
Scarce or controlled supplySo it keeps its value
Recognisable and hard to forgePeople trust it

Check what you just learned

1. Prices shown in a shop in rupees is an example of which function?
  • Unit of account (correct)
  • Store of value
  • Medium of exchange
  • Barter

A common yardstick for prices.

Tip

When someone says an asset 'is money', test it against the three functions rather than accepting or rejecting the label.

Check what you just learned

1. Saving for a trip next year uses money as:
  • A medium of exchange
  • A store of value (correct)
  • A unit of account
  • A barter good

Value is kept for later.
keyPoints: Money is a medium of exchange, a store of value and a unit of account.
Good money is durable, portable, divisible and trusted.

topics.title: From coins to bank apps to crypto
topics.html:
Most money today is already digital: your bank balance is an entry in a bank's database, and payment apps move those entries. Cryptocurrency differs in who keeps the record and who creates the money. Its record is a public blockchain kept by many participants, and new units are created by rules in software, not by a central bank.

Bank money and cryptocurrency
Bank moneyCryptocurrency (public chain)
Record keeperThe bankA distributed network
Who can use itAccount holders approved by the bankAnyone with a wallet
Supply decided byCentral bank and commercial banksSoftware rules, often a fixed schedule
ReversibleBanks can reverse some paymentsUsually final
Protection if you lose accessBank can help you recoverLost keys may mean lost funds

Check what you just learned

1. What mainly differs about cryptocurrency compared with bank money?
  • It is digital while bank money is not
  • It is always free
  • Who keeps the record and creates the money (correct)
  • It is always private

Both are digital; control differs.

Check what you just learned

1. A key difference between bank money and Bitcoin is:
  • Bitcoin is not digital
  • Bitcoin is a bank
  • Banks use blockchains only
  • Bitcoin's supply follows software rules rather than a central bank (correct)

Rules in code set the supply.
keyPoints: Most money is already digital.
Crypto changes who keeps the record and who creates the money.

topics.title: Why people use crypto, and why many do not
topics.html:
Reasons people use it
ReasonComment
Sending money across borders cheaply and quicklyCan help, especially where banking is costly; converting to local money still has costs
Access without a bank accountNeeds a phone and internet
Protection from inflation in unstable currenciesVolatility is a counter-risk
Open programmable financeOpportunities and risks
SpeculationThe largest driver for many; high risk of loss
Reasons many people do not
ReasonComment
Price volatilityLarge swings in value
Scams and hacksFrequent, with limited recourse
ComplexityKeys, addresses, fees and networks are hard for beginners
Regulatory uncertaintyRules differ and change
Irreversible mistakesA wrong address can mean lost money
Watch out

This course is education, not advice to buy anything. Most people who trade crypto actively lose money over time. Never invest money you cannot afford to lose, and never borrow to invest.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a real risk of using crypto?
  • Scams and irreversible mistakes (correct)
  • Transactions are always reversible
  • Prices never change
  • Banks guarantee deposits

Mistakes are usually final.

Check what you just learned

1. Sending crypto to a wrong address usually is:
  • Reversible by a bank
  • Irreversible (correct)
  • Free
  • Impossible

There is no central help desk.

Key terms: flip and sort

Medium of exchange
What people accept in payment
Store of value
Keeps purchasing power over time
Unit of account
A yardstick for prices
Inflation
A general rise in prices
Volatility
How much a price swings
Fiat money
Government-issued money not backed by a commodity
keyPoints: Reasons for and against are both real.
Most active traders lose money; risk is high.

modules.title: Types of digital assets
modules.summary: Native coins, tokens, stablecoins, central bank digital currencies and NFTs: what each is and what risks it carries.
modules.outcome: You can classify digital assets, explain how stablecoins try to keep their value and distinguish CBDCs from cryptocurrencies.
modules.intro: 'Crypto' covers many different things. A clear vocabulary stops you from treating a stablecoin like a speculative token or confusing a state digital currency with Bitcoin.

topics.title: Coins and tokens
topics.html:
Native coins and tokens
TypeDefinitionExamples (illustrative)
Native coinThe asset of a blockchain itself, used to pay fees and reward those who secure itBTC, ETH
TokenAn asset created by a smart contract on an existing blockchainStablecoins, governance tokens, loyalty points
Governance tokenGives holders votes on a project's decisionsUsed in some decentralised organisations
Utility tokenGives access to a serviceCredits for an app
Security tokenRepresents a financial claim and may be regulated as a securityTokenised shares or bonds

Labels are slippery. The same token might be called a utility token by its creators and treated as a security by a regulator. What matters is what rights it gives and what promises are made to buyers.

Check what you just learned

1. A token is:
  • The native currency of a chain
  • A mining machine
  • An asset created by a contract on an existing chain (correct)
  • A wallet

Built on a platform.

Check what you just learned

1. A governance token mainly gives holders:
  • Guaranteed profit
  • Free electricity
  • A bank account
  • Voting rights on decisions (correct)

A say in the project.
keyPoints: Coins are native to a chain; tokens are issued by contracts on a chain.
Legal treatment depends on rights and promises, not on the label.

topics.title: Stablecoins and CBDCs
topics.html:
Definition

Stablecoin. A token designed to keep a stable value, usually one unit of a currency such as the US dollar or the rupee. It tries to do this by holding reserves or collateral.

How stablecoins try to hold the peg
DesignHow it worksMain risk
Fiat-backedReserves of cash and short-term government securities back each tokenAre the reserves real, safe and audited? Can everyone redeem?
Crypto-backedOther crypto is locked as collateral, usually worth more than the tokens issuedA crash in collateral value
AlgorithmicCode adjusts supply to hold the price, with little or no backingDeath spirals; several have collapsed
Stablecoin versus CBDC
StablecoinCBDC
IssuerA private company or protocolThe central bank
Backed byReserves or collateralThe state; it is legal tender in digital form
BlockchainOften public chainsMay or may not use one
Main risksIssuer, reserves, pegPrivacy and state control debates
Watch out

'Stable' is a design goal, not a guarantee. Some stablecoins have lost their peg badly. Check what backs a stablecoin, who audits it and whether you can redeem it directly.

Check what you just learned

1. Which stablecoin design has collapsed most dramatically in the past?
  • Algorithmic with little backing (correct)
  • Fiat-backed with audited reserves
  • A CBDC
  • A bank deposit

Without real backing a peg can unravel.

Check what you just learned

1. A CBDC is issued by:
  • A private exchange
  • A central bank (correct)
  • A miner
  • A wallet company

A state digital currency.
keyPoints: Stablecoins try to hold a peg using reserves, collateral or algorithms.
A CBDC is issued by a central bank; a stablecoin by a private issuer.

topics.title: NFTs and tokenised assets
topics.html:
A non-fungible token (NFT) is a unique token on a blockchain. Because each is distinct, it can represent a specific item: a piece of digital art, a ticket, a certificate, or a record linked to something in the real world.

What an NFT is and is not
IsIs not
A record on a chain that a particular address owns a particular tokenAutomatically a copyright transfer; ownership of the token does not always mean ownership of the underlying work
Able to be bought, sold and used in appsA guarantee that the linked image or file will stay available; many store files off-chain
Useful for tickets, memberships, credentialsA guaranteed investment; many NFTs lost most of their value

Questions before dealing with an NFT

  1. What exactly do I get: a licence, the artwork, or just the token?
  2. Where is the file stored, and what if that service closes?
  3. Who made it, and can I verify that they are the real creator?
  4. Are fees and royalties clear?
  5. Is it an impulse or a considered choice?

Check what you just learned

1. Owning an NFT automatically gives you:
  • The copyright to the work
  • A guaranteed profit
  • A recorded token, but not always the copyright (correct)
  • A bank loan

Rights depend on the terms.

Check what you just learned

1. An NFT is described as 'non-fungible' because:
  • It cannot be sold
  • It is a coin
  • It is free
  • Each one is unique (correct)

Not interchangeable.

Key terms: flip and sort

Native coin
The base asset of a blockchain
Token
An asset made by a smart contract
Stablecoin
A token designed to hold a stable value
Peg
The value a stablecoin aims to keep
CBDC
Central bank digital currency
NFT
Non-fungible token
keyPoints: An NFT is a unique token, often linked to files stored elsewhere.
Rights come from terms and law, not from the token alone.

modules.title: Wallets and exchanges
modules.summary: How people buy, hold and move crypto, and what each choice costs and risks.
modules.outcome: You can compare custodial and non-custodial storage, understand exchange orders and fees and calculate the real cost of a trade.
modules.intro: Buying crypto is easy; doing it safely is a skill. This module explains the places where crypto is held and traded, the costs hidden in each step and the habits that protect you.

topics.title: Where your crypto lives
topics.html:
Storage choices
ChoiceWho holds the keysProsCons
Exchange account (custodial)The companyEasy; recovery by support; simple to tradeYou trust the company; exchanges can fail or be hacked; accounts can be frozen
Software wallet (hot, non-custodial)YouYou control the funds; easy to use with appsConnected to the internet; exposed to malware and phishing
Hardware wallet (cold, non-custodial)You, offlineKeys never touch your computer; best protection for larger amountsCosts money; backup is your job
Paper or metal backup of the recovery phraseYouOffline and cheapCan be lost or damaged; must be stored securely

A common approach is to keep a small 'spending' amount in a software wallet or exchange and move savings you are holding for the long term to a hardware wallet. Whatever you choose, the biggest risk is usually human: phishing, losing the phrase, or being tricked into approving something.

Check what you just learned

1. Which storage option keeps the keys offline?
  • Hardware wallet (correct)
  • Exchange account
  • Browser extension
  • Mobile app

Signing happens on the device.

Watch out

'Not your keys, not your coins' is a slogan with truth in it: if a company holds your keys, you depend on its honesty, solvency and security.

Check what you just learned

1. A common safe habit for larger long-term holdings is to use:
  • An exchange only
  • A hardware wallet (correct)
  • A screenshot
  • An email

Keys stay offline.
keyPoints: Custodial storage trades control for convenience; non-custodial storage does the reverse.
Hardware wallets keep keys offline.

topics.title: Exchanges, orders and KYC
topics.html:
Types of exchange
TypeHow it works
Centralised exchange (CEX)A company matches buyers and sellers, holds your funds, and must usually verify your identity (KYC)
Decentralised exchange (DEX)Smart contracts let you swap from your own wallet with no company holding the funds; you take on contract and market risks
Peer-to-peer platformsMatch individual buyers and sellers, often using an escrow
Order types
OrderMeaningUse
Market orderBuy or sell now at the best available priceSpeed, but you may get a worse price (slippage)
Limit orderBuy or sell only at your chosen price or betterControl over price, but it may not fill
Stop orderTriggers a trade if the price reaches a levelLimit losses; can trigger at bad prices in a fast market
Definition

Spread. The gap between the best price someone will pay (bid) and the lowest price someone will accept (ask). Buying at the ask and selling at the bid costs you the spread.

Definition

KYC. 'Know your customer': identity checks that regulated platforms perform to meet legal rules against fraud and money laundering.

Check what you just learned

1. Which order guarantees the price but not that the trade happens?
  • Market order
  • Instant swap
  • Limit order (correct)
  • Airdrop

It fills only at your price or better.

Check what you just learned

1. KYC stands for:
  • Keep your coins
  • Kilobyte check
  • Key yield control
  • Know your customer (correct)

Identity verification.
keyPoints: Exchanges differ in who holds your funds and how they are regulated.
Market orders give speed; limit orders give price control.

topics.title: The real cost of a trade
topics.html:
A headline 'zero fee' is rarely zero cost. A round trip, buying and then selling, can include a trading fee each time, the spread each time, network fees for moving funds, and withdrawal fees.

Formula · Round-trip cost

cost ≈ 2 × (fee + half-spread) × amount + flat fees

With a 0.5% fee, a 0.3% half-spread and a 150-rupee withdrawal on 50,000 rupees, the cost is about 0.8% on each side plus 150, around 950 rupees.

Round-trip cost calculator

Change the amount, fee, spread and flat fee to see what you lose on a buy and sell with no price change. Teaching figures, not any exchange's real fees.

Adjust Amount (rupees), Fee per trade (%), Half-spread per trade (%), Flat withdrawal fee (rupees) and see Value after the buy, Total round-trip cost (rupees), Cost as a share of the amount (%) change.

Tip

Small amounts suffer most from flat fees. Check the full fee schedule before you start.

Check what you just learned

1. Why can a 'zero trading fee' still cost you money?
  • Spreads and other fees still apply (correct)
  • It cannot
  • Because of taxes only
  • Because of weather

There are other costs.

Check what you just learned

1. A round trip means:
  • Travelling to an exchange
  • Buying and later selling (correct)
  • Sending to a friend
  • Mining a block

Both legs carry costs.

Key terms: flip and sort

Custodial
A company holds your keys
Hot wallet
Keys on a device connected to the internet
Cold storage
Keys kept offline
Spread
Gap between buy and sell prices
Slippage
A worse price than expected on a fast order
KYC
Identity checks required by regulated platforms
keyPoints: Count fees, spread and flat charges on both sides of a trade.
Small trades are hit hardest by flat fees.

modules.title: Markets and risk
modules.summary: Why crypto prices swing, how to measure risk, and the habits that protect you from yourself.
modules.outcome: You can calculate returns and volatility, compare dollar-cost averaging with a lump sum and recognise the mental traps that cost investors money.
modules.intro: Crypto assets are among the most volatile things you can hold. This module teaches you to measure that volatility instead of fearing or ignoring it, and to design your own limits. It is education about risk, not advice to invest.

topics.title: Returns and volatility
topics.html:
Formula · Return

return = (new price ÷ old price) − 1

A price moving from 100 to 112 is a return of 112 ÷ 100 − 1 = 12%.

Formula · Volatility

volatility = standard deviation of returns

A larger standard deviation means the returns are more spread out: bigger swings in both directions.

Price swings and what they do to you

Change a loss and see the gain you need just to get back to even. Losses hurt more than the same-sized gains help.

Adjust Fall in price (%) and see Gain needed to recover (%), Value of 10,000 rupees after the fall change.

This asymmetry is why large drawdowns matter so much: a 50% fall needs a 100% rise to recover. High volatility means a real chance of large falls even in assets that rise over the long term.

Check what you just learned

1. After a 50% fall, what gain is needed to get back to the starting value?
  • 25%
  • 50%
  • 100% (correct)
  • 200%

Half of the original needs to double.

Check what you just learned

1. A price moves from 80 to 100. The return is:
  • 20%
  • 125%
  • 80%
  • 25% (correct)

100/80 − 1 = 25%.
keyPoints: Return = new ÷ old − 1; volatility is the spread of returns.
A 50% fall needs a 100% rise to recover.

topics.title: Diversification, position size and averaging
topics.html:
Risk tools
ToolIdeaLimit
Position sizingPut only an amount you could lose entirely at riskNeeds discipline
DiversificationSpread across different assets so one failure hurts lessMany crypto assets move together in a crash; it does not remove risk
Dollar-cost averagingInvest a fixed amount at regular intervalsReduces timing risk; does not guarantee profit
RebalancingPeriodically restore your intended mixCan cost fees and taxes

Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) spreads purchases across time so you do not have to guess the best moment. When prices fall you automatically buy more units; when they rise you buy fewer. Over a rising market a lump sum made earlier usually wins; over a falling or choppy market DCA can look better. Neither is a certainty.

DCA versus lump sum

Two prices decide who wins: the price at the start and the price at the end. Change them and compare (a simple two-purchase model).

Adjust Price at purchase 1, Price at purchase 2, Price at the end and see Units: 2,000 split in two (DCA), Units: 2,000 at once, End value of DCA, End value of lump sum change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does diversifying across many crypto assets not remove risk?
  • Many of them fall together in a crash (correct)
  • It does
  • They are all the same coin
  • It is illegal

Correlation rises in stress.

Check what you just learned

1. Dollar-cost averaging means:
  • Investing all at once
  • Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals (correct)
  • Selling when prices rise
  • Avoiding fees

Spreads purchases over time.
keyPoints: Size positions so a total loss is survivable.
DCA reduces timing risk but does not guarantee profit.

topics.title: Mental traps
topics.html:
Common behavioural traps
TrapWhat it looks likeA counter
FOMOBuying because the price is rising and others are talking about itDecide your rules before the hype; wait a day
Panic sellingSelling everything after a sharp fallSet position sizes you can live with; avoid checking constantly
AnchoringWaiting to 'get back to even' regardless of the outlookAsk: would I buy it today at this price?
Herd followingCopying friends or influencersCheck incentives: do they profit if you buy?
Overconfidence after a winTaking bigger risks after a lucky gainReview your process, not just the outcome
Gambler's chasingDoubling up to win back lossesStop; losses are sunk

Common mistakes

  • Using leverage or borrowed money.
  • Following an influencer without checking their incentives and disclosures.
  • Trading on feeling instead of a written plan.

Check what you just learned

1. Doubling your bet to win back losses is called:
  • Diversification
  • Rebalancing
  • Chasing losses (correct)
  • Staking

A classic gambling trap.

Tip

Write your rules down when you are calm: how much, what you will hold, and when you will review. Then follow them when you are not calm.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a sensible counter to FOMO?
  • Buy immediately
  • Follow the crowd
  • Borrow money
  • Decide your rules in advance and wait (correct)

Slow down.

Key terms: flip and sort

Return
Percentage change in price
Volatility
Spread of returns
Drawdown
A fall from a previous peak
Diversification
Spreading risk across assets
DCA
Dollar-cost averaging
Leverage
Using borrowed money to increase exposure
keyPoints: FOMO, panic, anchoring and herd behaviour are predictable traps.
Write rules in advance and follow them under pressure.

modules.title: Tokenomics and due diligence
modules.summary: How a token's supply and incentives are designed, and how to investigate before trusting a project.
modules.outcome: You can read a vesting schedule, calculate circulating supply and write a structured due-diligence note.
modules.intro: Two tokens with the same price can be very different bets. Tokenomics, the design of supply and incentives, shows who holds what, when more tokens arrive and who benefits. Due diligence turns that into a decision about whether to trust a project.

topics.title: Supply, allocation and unlocks
topics.html:
Key tokenomics terms
TermMeaning
Total supplyAll tokens that exist or will ever exist under the rules
Circulating supplyTokens currently available to trade
Max supplyThe cap, if there is one
Market capitalisationPrice × circulating supply
Fully diluted valuationPrice × total (or max) supply
VestingA schedule releasing tokens over time
CliffA period before any tokens unlock
Emissions or inflationNew tokens created by the protocol over time
Formula · Market cap and FDV

market cap = price × circulating supply; FDV = price × total supply

If only 30% of tokens circulate, the fully diluted valuation is more than three times the market cap.

Market cap versus fully diluted value

Change the price and the share of tokens in circulation to see how the headline market cap can hide future supply.

Adjust Price (rupees), Total supply (millions), Share circulating (%) and see Market cap (millions of rupees), Fully diluted value (millions of rupees), FDV divided by market cap change.

When a large block of locked tokens unlocks, new supply can reach the market and push the price down if holders sell. Looking at the unlock calendar is a basic check.

Check what you just learned

1. Fully diluted valuation is price multiplied by:
  • Total or maximum supply (correct)
  • Circulating supply
  • Trading volume
  • Number of wallets

It counts tokens not yet unlocked.

Check what you just learned

1. A cliff in vesting means:
  • Tokens unlock instantly
  • No tokens unlock for an initial period (correct)
  • Tokens are burned
  • The price falls

Nothing is released before the cliff.
keyPoints: Market cap uses circulating supply; FDV uses total supply.
Vesting and unlock dates affect future supply.

topics.title: Incentives and red flags
topics.html:
Healthy and worrying signs
HealthyWorrying
Team and investor tokens vest over several yearsInsiders hold a large share, unlocked at launch
Clear rules on creating new tokensUnlimited minting by the team with no limits stated
The token has a clear job in the productThe token's only purpose is to be bought
Public, independent auditsNo audit, or audits by unknown firms
Honest discussion of risksPromises of guaranteed returns
Open code and active community scrutinyHidden code, anonymous team, urgency to buy

Ask who benefits when you buy. If returns to early buyers are paid from new buyers' money, the structure resembles a Ponzi or pyramid scheme, which is illegal in many countries and always collapses when new money slows.

Watch out

No legitimate project can guarantee returns, and no investment 'cannot lose'. Treat any such promise as a reason to walk away.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a strong warning sign?
  • A public audit
  • A vesting schedule
  • Guaranteed monthly returns (correct)
  • An open-source repository

Returns cannot be guaranteed.

Check what you just learned

1. Returns paid from new buyers' money resemble:
  • A bank
  • A tax rebate
  • A grant
  • A Ponzi scheme (correct)

They collapse when new money stops.
keyPoints: Check who holds the supply, when it unlocks and what gives the token value.
Guaranteed returns signal fraud.

topics.title: A due-diligence routine
topics.html:
Where to look
QuestionSources
ClaimsOfficial documentation and whitepaper
TeamPublic profiles with a verifiable record
Code and auditsPublic repository; audit reports from known firms
SupplyBlock explorer, official tokenomics page
Legal and regulatoryRegulator websites; qualified advisers
Independent viewsNeutral research, not paid promotion

Write it down

  1. A short note forces you to see what you do and do not know.
  2. Record the red flags and decide your verdict before you buy.
  3. If you cannot explain the project in two sentences, do not invest.

Check what you just learned

1. Which source is least reliable for assessing a project?
  • Paid promotion by influencers (correct)
  • Public audit report
  • The code repository
  • Official documentation

Paid promotion has an incentive.

Check what you just learned

1. A good reason to avoid a project is that:
  • You can explain it in two sentences
  • You cannot explain how it makes money (correct)
  • It has an audit
  • It is open source

If you cannot explain it, do not invest.

Key terms: flip and sort

Tokenomics
The design of a token's supply and incentives
Circulating supply
Tokens available to trade
FDV
Fully diluted valuation
Vesting
Gradual release of locked tokens
Cliff
Initial period with no unlock
Due diligence
Investigating before trusting
keyPoints: Follow claims, team, code, supply and legality.
Write a note and decide before buying.

modules.title: Rules, tax and safety
modules.summary: The legal and practical habits that keep you safe, compliant and calm.
modules.outcome: You can describe the main areas of crypto regulation, keep useful records and write a personal plan with limits.
modules.intro: Crypto sits between technology and finance, and the rules are changing in most countries. This final module is about habits: staying on the right side of the law, protecting yourself from fraud and deciding your own limits.

topics.title: How regulation approaches crypto
topics.html:
Areas regulators look at
AreaTypical concern
Exchanges and custodiansLicensing, safeguarding customer funds, reporting
Anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism financingIdentity checks and monitoring (KYC and AML)
Consumer protectionMisleading adverts, scams, risk warnings
Securities and financial productsWhether a token is an investment contract
TaxationWhether gains, income or payments are taxable
Stablecoins and paymentsReserves, redemption rights, stability

Countries take different approaches: some have detailed licensing, some restrict or ban certain activities, and some are still developing their rules. Because rules change, rely on current official sources and on a qualified adviser, not on social media.

Watch out

This course gives general education, not legal, tax or investment advice.

Check what you just learned

1. Why do regulated exchanges ask for ID?
  • To raise prices
  • To slow you down
  • To meet anti-money-laundering and fraud rules (correct)
  • To advertise

KYC is a legal requirement.

Check what you just learned

1. The best source for current crypto rules is:
  • A random chat group
  • An anonymous post
  • A meme
  • Official regulators and qualified advisers (correct)

Rules change.
keyPoints: Regulators focus on exchanges, AML, consumers, securities, tax and stablecoins.
Rules differ by country and change; check official sources.

topics.title: Records and tax
topics.html:
In many countries, selling crypto, swapping one asset for another, spending it, or earning it (for example as pay or rewards) can be taxable events. The details differ widely, so the single most useful habit is to keep clear records.

What to record
ItemWhy
Date and timeNeeded to work out gains and holding periods
Asset and quantityWhat was traded
Price in your local currencyTo compute gain or loss
Fees paidMay reduce a gain
Wallet addresses and exchange namesTo prove ownership and trace transfers
Reason for the transactionPurchase, sale, swap, gift, income
Worked example

A simple gain

You bought 0.5 units for 20,000 rupees and later sold them for 26,000, paying 300 in fees.

  1. Proceeds: 26,000.
  2. Cost: 20,000.
  3. Fees: 300.
  4. Gain before tax: 26,000 − 20,000 − 300 = 5,700.

Answer. Whether and how this is taxed depends on your country's rules.

Tip

Export your exchange history regularly; platforms can disappear and records are harder to rebuild later.

Check what you just learned

1. Which habit helps most at tax time?
  • Keeping dated records of every transaction (correct)
  • Deleting your history
  • Using many exchanges at random
  • Ignoring fees

Records make reporting accurate.

Check what you just learned

1. A realised gain is computed from:
  • Only the sale price
  • Proceeds minus cost minus fees (correct)
  • Only the purchase price
  • The date alone

Net of cost and fees.
keyPoints: Keep dated records with prices, fees and addresses.
Tax treatment differs by country; ask a professional.

topics.title: Your personal plan
topics.html:
What a good personal plan contains

  1. A maximum amount: only what you could lose entirely.
  2. Where and how you will store it, and who could find your backups.
  3. What you will never do: borrow, follow strangers, share your recovery phrase.
  4. How you will research before any purchase.
  5. When you will review, and what would make you stop.
  6. A note to check tax and legal rules for your country.
Warning signs that you are not in control
SignAction
Checking prices constantly and losing sleepReduce your position and take a break
Borrowing or using money needed for billsStop and seek advice
Hiding losses from familyTalk to someone you trust
Chasing losses with bigger betsStop; consider help
Watch out

If trading is affecting your mental health or finances, speak to a trusted person or a professional counsellor, and use the self-exclusion tools that many platforms offer.

Check what you just learned

1. The maximum you should risk is:
  • Your savings
  • Whatever a friend invests
  • An amount you could lose entirely without harm (correct)
  • Borrowed money

Never risk what you cannot afford to lose.

Check what you just learned

1. A healthy plan includes:
  • No limits
  • Following strangers
  • Borrowing
  • A maximum amount and a review date (correct)

Rules protect you from yourself.

Realised gain
Profit after selling

An action that can create tax

A tool to stop yourself trading

Following rules and laws
